relations.note: AICH of a single block is SHA-1, and SHA1lsb35 is SHA-1 with the leading nibbles masked to zero, so any tool that ignores that field -- hashcat -m 100 skips positions 0-7 and john Raw-SHA1-Linkedin skips 0-4, measured 2026-09-01, and the mask is 5 nibbles wide -- reports one for the other. They agree on every input outside those nibbles and differ nowhere else that such a tool looks.

tool_note.hashcat: proven three ways because -m 100 alone is not enough: hashcat cracked this row's own vector under mode 100, john's Raw-SHA1 and dynamic_26 cracked it too with a FULL digest comparison, and Digest::SHA confirms sha1("password123") is cbfdac6008f9cab4083784cbd1874f76618d2a97 character for character. The third step is required here: measured 2026-08-31, hashcat -m 100 skips hash positions 0-7, so on its own it cannot tell this row from sha1lsb35, which is the same digest with those nibbles masked. discover-hashcat.pl's canary withheld the claim for exactly that reason; this is a human overriding it with the independent recomputation, not the tool's word.
tool_note.john: format discovered by round-trip search, not by name. Raw-SHA1-Linkedin was recorded here by discover-john.pl on 2026-08-31 and WITHDRAWN the same day. It is john's format for the LinkedIn leak, whose hashes have their leading nibbles zeroed, and it ignores hash positions 0-4 -- the 20 bits that leak zeroed -- measured position by position on 2026-09-01. That is the same defect the hashcat canary found in -m 100, at a different width: -m 100 skips 0-7. It therefore cracks any full SHA-1 digest as well, which is a collision and not a denotation. Raw-SHA1 and dynamic_26 both compare the whole digest and were re-checked position by position.

This entry carried the expression "sha256($s.$p)(hMailServer)", transcribed from the hx Language Specification $Revision: 1.15$ (Waffle, Aug 2026), Appendix A entry for mdxfind type HMAILSERVER (e860) by a parser that has since been corrected: it carries a parenthesised group after what is already a complete expression, which is how a prose gloss reaches the data; and it carries the bare operand hMailServer, which john's dynamic language cannot bind. Nothing can compile that string, so it was a claim rather than a fact, and it is withdrawn rather than adjusted -- guessing what upstream meant is exactly what the expression field exists to stop. entries.notes: This row is mdxfind type MD5CAPMD5USER. CORRECTED TWICE on 2026-08-31, and the second correction matters more than the first. Waffle named the unknown vector d4f7dec5...:abc123 as the colon form, confirmed here by independent Digest::MD5 and by local mdxfind pinned to ^MD5CAPMD5USER$ with -F. But the hx specification (rev 1.15) Appendix A Note [24] then showed the stronger fact: MD5CAPMD5USER is a MULTI-EMIT type. It emits BOTH md5(cap(md5($p)).$u) and md5(cap(md5($p)).":".$u) and matches if either reproduces the stored digest. So this row is not one computation, and neither of its two vectors is anomalous -- 05b56c69... is the colonless emit and d4f7dec5... is the colon emit. The first correction here wrongly called the colonless vector foreign and removed it; it is restored. A copy also sits on md5-md5-pass-salt, which is the row for the colonless construction in its own right. john has no format for either emit: discover-john.pl ran all 957 formats against the colon vector with zero matches, and the dynamic language has no literal-string token. The 198,534-construction sweep that failed to identify this missed it because it enumerated terms and never a literal separator.

relations.note: MD5MD5USER and MD5CAPMD5USER differ only by cap() on the inner hex digest, which is a no-op whenever that digest starts with a digit. md5('rosetta') is 975790df..., so both types reproduce this shared vector identically; they diverge on any plaintext whose md5 starts with a letter.

tool_note.john: no john format reproduces this construction: discover-john.pl ran all 957 formats (439 CPU + 518 disabled dynamics) against this entry's vector in 38.5s with zero matches, 2026-08-31. Separately, the dynamic expression compiler cannot express it either -- it has no literal-string token. The dynamic_1007/2006/6 this entry used to name belong to the colonless md5(md5($p).$s) and do not crack this vector.

There is therefore no single expression to record, and writing one of the emitted forms into expression: would be a false claim even though the string itself is correct. This is also why two vectors of such a type can disagree with each other, and why a tool matching one of them is not evidence about the other.

entries.name: MD5UCBASE64SHA1RAW
entries.notes: The vendored catalog renders this type's example digest in uppercase hex, and mdxfind will not read it back in that case, so the seeding pass could not verify it. mdxfind -z computes the same digest in lowercase for the same plaintext, and pinned to ^MD5UCBASE64SHA1RAW$ it reproduces that form; the stored vector is the catalog's own digest re-cased, not one we invented. Fourteen other types carry an uppercase example (MD5UC, SHA1UC, SHA256UC, RACF, ORACLE7 among them) and are NOT all the same story -- MD5UC and SHA256UC do not reproduce in either case.

relations.note: AICH of a single block is SHA-1, and SHA1lsb35 is SHA-1 with the leading nibbles masked to zero, so any tool that ignores that field -- hashcat -m 100 skips positions 0-7 and john Raw-SHA1-Linkedin skips 0-4, measured 2026-09-01, and the mask is 5 nibbles wide -- reports one for the other. They agree on every input outside those nibbles and differ nowhere else that such a tool looks.

SHA1UC is SHA-1 written in uppercase hex and SHA1lsb35 is SHA-1 with the leading nibbles masked to zero, so a tool that skips that field cannot tell them apart: hashcat -m 100 skips hash positions 0-7 and john Raw-SHA1-Linkedin skips 0-4, measured 2026-09-01. SHA1lsb35 masks exactly 5 nibbles, so either blind spot covers the whole difference: the digests are identical from position 5 onward.

relations.note: SHA1UC is SHA-1 written in uppercase hex and SHA1lsb35 is SHA-1 with the leading nibbles masked to zero, so a tool that skips that field cannot tell them apart: hashcat -m 100 skips hash positions 0-7 and john Raw-SHA1-Linkedin skips 0-4, measured 2026-09-01. tool_note.hashcat: proven three ways because -m 100 alone is not enough: hashcat cracked this row's own vector under mode 100, john's Raw-SHA1 and dynamic_26 cracked it too with a FULL digest comparison, and Digest::SHA confirms sha1("password123") is cbfdac6008f9cab4083784cbd1874f76618d2a97 character for character. The third step is required here: measured 2026-08-31, hashcat -m 100 skips hash positions 0-7, so on its own it cannot tell this row from sha1lsb35, which is the same digest with those nibbles masked. discover-hashcat.pl's canary withheld the claim for exactly that reason; this is a human overriding it with the independent recomputation, not the tool's word.
tool_note.john: format discovered by round-trip search, not by name. Raw-SHA1-Linkedin was recorded here by discover-john.pl on 2026-08-31 and WITHDRAWN the same day. It is john's format for the LinkedIn leak, whose hashes have their leading nibbles zeroed, and it ignores hash positions 0-4 -- the 20 bits that leak zeroed -- measured position by position on 2026-09-01. That is the same defect the hashcat canary found in -m 100, at a different width: -m 100 skips 0-7. It therefore cracks any full SHA-1 digest as well, which is a collision and not a denotation. Raw-SHA1 and dynamic_26 both compare the whole digest and were re-checked position by position.
